## The Problem: Few Expensive Tests

Your job: tune parameters, but you face:

- Only about **fifteen expensive** experiments allowed
- **Many interacting** parameters — more than ten
- Change one, the others move — can't tune one at a time
- So: spend a tiny budget in the **smartest way**?

## Why It Is Hard: Black Box \& Budget

- **Black box**: you see input and output, never the inside
- **Budget**: only fifteen precise runs, but a huge space
- Task: find the **best point** of a high-dimensional black box

## The Key Idea: Two Channels

Good news — our black box has two channels:

$$
h_k(\boldsymbol{x}) = h_{k-1}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \delta_k(\boldsymbol{x})
$$

- **Cheap** channel: run many times, but **biased**
- **Expensive** channel: only 15 runs, accurate
- Idea: combine — accurate = cheap + a correction

## Tool 1: Maxpro Design

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Maxpro criterion:

$$
\min_D \sum_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^p (x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2}
$$

- Start **evenly**: spread out in **every projection**
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![Maxpro design](../figures/2.pdf){width=100%}
:::
:::

## Tool 2: The Stand-In Model (Gaussian Process)

- A **Gaussian process** is a normal distribution over **whole functions** — not one number
- It predicts a value **and** an **uncertainty** at every point
- Uncertainty tells us **where to test next**: hopeful \& unsure

## The Whole Pipeline

1. **Spread out** the starting points
2. Feed in many **cheap** runs $\rightarrow$ a **rough map**
3. Send **one expensive** run to the predicted valley
4. **Repeat** — the map gets sharper every round

## Our Question

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{x}} \approx \argmin_{\boldsymbol{x}\in[0,1]^p} h_\mathrm{H}(\boldsymbol{x})
$$

- Goal: minimize the expensive function with only **15 precise runs**
- Three small questions:
  - Does **combining the channels** help?
  - Does **screening** the parameters help?
  - Does it still work **in high dimensions**?

## Answer 1: Combination Is the Key

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Combination is the key](../figures/3.pdf){width=100%}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Metric: **median** of the best found over 20 repeats — lower is better
- Cheap + precise **beats** precise alone
- 1-D: precise alone stuck at 0; with fusion $\rightarrow$ **global optimum**
- 2-D: lands right next to the **known answer**
:::
:::

## Answer 2: Screening Is Useless

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Screening is useless](../figures/4.pdf){width=100%}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Screening **ranks** parameters by cheap runs
- But cheap runs are **biased** $\rightarrow$ ranking is unreliable
- Result: **removing** screening actually helps
:::
:::

## Answer 3: High Dimensions Fail

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![High dimensions fail](../figures/5.pdf){width=100%}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- In 8-D, fusion **collapses** too
- Too few precise points to **sketch an 8-D landscape**
- Fusion is decisive — but it has a **ceiling**
:::
:::

## The Whole Picture

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![All results](../figures/6.pdf){height=65%}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Low dims: full pipeline wins; drop fusion $\rightarrow$ breaks
- High dims: **nothing works**
- One line: **make every precise test count**; limit = dimensionality
:::
:::

## Future Directions

My Future Directions:

1. **When is screening trustworthy**? — find the bias conditions
2. **Tame high dimensions**? — add structure, or reduce dimension first
3. **Real-world tool**: give it a budget — get the best plan

## Summary

- Not "more precise runs" — but "**more value per run**"
- Limit: the **curse of high dimensions**
